overview: Microraptor gui was the size of a crow but carried flight feathers on all four limbs — both arms and legs — making it the strongest evidence that the evolution of flight in dinosaurs may have passed through a four-winged stage. Iridescent black plumage has been reconstructed from melanosomes preserved in its feathers, making it one of the few dinosaurs whose colour can be described with confidence.

Hundreds of Microraptor specimens are known from the Yixian Formation of Liaoning, China (~125–120 Ma), making it among the most studied small dinosaurs. Stomach contents preserved in several specimens include fish, lizards and the remains of a small bird, revealing an opportunistic diet despite its tiny size.

fossilSites.name: Yixian Formation
fossilSites.note: Lower Cretaceous lacustrine deposits with hundreds of Microraptor specimens; the world's premier feathered dinosaur site.

articles.title: Four wings and flight origin
articles.body: Feathers on the hindlimbs form aerodynamic surfaces comparable to those on the wings, creating a biplane-like lifting surface. Aerodynamic modelling suggests Microraptor was capable of controlled gliding and possibly powered flight from a perched position. Its discovery reopened the debate between arboreal ("trees-down") and cursorial ("ground-up") flight origins, suggesting a complex mosaic rather than a simple linear transition.

articles.title: Plumage and coloration
articles.body: Analysis of fossilised melanosomes — melanin-bearing organelles preserved in exceptional Yixian specimens — revealed an iridescent black colour similar to a modern starling or magpie. This is only the second dinosaur (after Anchiornis) to have its colour pattern reconstructed from direct chemical evidence rather than inference.

articles.title: Ecology
articles.body: Despite its small size Microraptor was a versatile predator. Known stomach contents include fish bones and scales, lizard remains and a small enantiornithine bird — indicating it could hunt in multiple microhabitats. Its large eyes suggest crepuscular or low-light activity; its small size placed it in direct competition with early birds for arboreal and aerial prey.

fossilRecord.material: Many feathered specimens preserving flight feathers on arms and legs.
fossilRecord.evidence: Feather impressions and stomach contents provide direct evidence for plumage, gliding/flying ability and varied diet.

record.description: Microraptor was a small feathered dromaeosaurid from the Jiufotang Formation of Liaoning, known from hundreds of articulated specimens, especially M. gui; species limits within the genus remain debated.
facts: Long flight feathers on arms and legs form a four-winged aerodynamic configuration.
Aerodynamic studies support gliding or some aerial capacity, while launch and powered-flight performance remain debated.
Gut contents document a varied carnivorous diet including birds, mammals, lizards and fish in different specimens.

presentation.heroLead: A crow-sized, four-winged dromaeosaurid from the Jehol lake beds of China, known from hundreds of feathered skeletons that document its plumage, colour and even its last meals.

heroMedia.title: Life restoration of Microraptor gui
heroMedia.alt: Life restoration of Microraptor gui with long flight feathers on both the arms and the legs
heroMedia.caption: Life restoration by Fred Wierum. The four-winged plumage and glossy dark colouring follow fossil evidence; posture in flight is interpretive.

animalParagraphs: Microraptor was a small dromaeosaurid, about the size of a crow, with a long bony tail ending in a fan of feathers. Its most remarkable feature is a set of long, asymmetrical flight feathers on the hindlimbs as well as the arms, producing a four-winged layout with no living equivalent.

The plumage is directly preserved in many specimens. Analysis of fossil melanosomes in one skeleton indicates that the feathers were predominantly black with an iridescent sheen, comparable to a modern grackle or crow. Gut contents in different individuals include a bird, a mammal, a lizard and a fish, so its diet was clearly varied.

How Microraptor used its wings is still debated. Wind-tunnel and modelling studies agree that it could glide or parachute effectively, but whether it could launch from the ground or flap in powered flight remains an open question.
animalHighlights: Long flight feathers on the legs as well as the arms are preserved on many specimens, giving a four-winged body plan.
Melanosome evidence indicates predominantly black, iridescent plumage in at least one individual.
Preserved stomach contents from separate specimens document prey ranging from birds and mammals to lizards and fish.

lifeCards.label: Feeding
lifeCards.reason: Different specimens preserve a bird, a mammal, a lizard and a fish in the gut region, showing an opportunistic diet.

lifeCards.label: Movement
lifeCards.reason: Asymmetrical flight feathers and aerodynamic modelling support gliding at least; powered flight and take-off ability are inferred, not observed.

lifeCards.label: Known size
lifeCards.reason: Complete skeletons fix the length, but body mass of roughly a kilogram is an estimate and the sample includes animals of different growth stages.

lifeCards.label: Appearance
lifeCards.reason: Plumage outline is directly preserved; the black iridescent colour comes from melanosome analysis of a single individual and may not represent every animal.

locality.name: Jiufotang Formation lake beds
locality.note: Fine-grained lake sediments of the Jehol Group. The map shows the Chaoyang region rather than an individual quarry, as many specimens come from local collectors.

presentation.classificationSummary: Microraptor is a dromaeosaurid within Microraptorinae, a group of small, often four-winged dromaeosaurs from the Early Cretaceous of China. Three species have been named, M. zhaoianus, M. gui and M. hanqingi, but many workers regard them as a single variable species.

related.reason: Compare with a feathered dromaeosaurid from the older Yixian Formation of Liaoning.
Compare with an earlier four-winged paravian whose colour has also been reconstructed.
Compare with a larger, ground-living dromaeosaurid from the Late Cretaceous of Mongolia.

questions.title: Could it fly under its own power?
questions.copy: Gliding is well supported. Whether the shoulder allowed a full flight stroke and whether it could launch from the ground remain contested.

questions.title: How many species are there?
questions.copy: Differences between M. zhaoianus, M. gui and M. hanqingi may reflect growth, individual variation or preservation rather than separate species.

questions.title: Was every Microraptor black?
questions.copy: The iridescent black colour is based on melanosomes from one specimen. Other individuals, sexes or ages might have differed.

review.ageReviewNote: The main Jiufotang sample is Aptian, close to 120 Ma; species and localities should not be merged into a broader generic range without review.

Powered flight versus gliding remains debated.

evidence.material: Hundreds of articulated feathered skeletons, several with gut contents.
evidence.confidenceLimit: Aerial capacity is well supported but exact flight stroke, launch mode and species-wide colour vary by specimen.
evidence.summary: Microraptor was a small feathered dromaeosaurid from the Jiufotang Formation of Liaoning, known from hundreds of articulated specimens, especially M. gui; species limits within the genus remain debated.
evidence.sourceBasis: Xu et al. (2003), four-winged Microraptor from China; O'Connor et al. (2011), Microraptor with ingested bird remains

specimens.name: Holotype of M. zhaoianus
specimens.institution: Institute of Vertebrate Paleontology and Paleoanthropology, Beijing
specimens.note: Partial articulated skeleton, the name-bearing specimen of the genus (Xu, Zhou and Wang 2000).

specimens.name: Holotype of M. gui
specimens.institution: Institute of Vertebrate Paleontology and Paleoanthropology, Beijing
specimens.note: Near-complete skeleton with hindlimb flight feathers (Xu et al. 2003); many workers treat M. gui as a synonym of M. zhaoianus.

panel.headline: Hundreds of feathered skeletons from the Jehol lake beds.
panel.standfirst: Microraptor is one of the most abundantly sampled non-avian dinosaurs. Articulated, feather-bearing skeletons on limestone slabs preserve the plumage outline, melanosomes and stomach contents alongside the bones.

coverage.label: Excellent
coverage.basis: Every skeletal region is represented by many articulated individuals, with feathers preserved in place on numerous slabs.

knownRemains.title: What is actually preserved?
knownRemains.summary: Complete skulls, vertebral columns, girdles and limbs from many individuals, together with the outlines of arm, leg and tail feathers, fossil melanosomes and, in several specimens, the remains of prey in the gut.
knownRemains.note: Jehol fossils are crushed flat on slabs, so three-dimensional skull and joint anatomy is harder to study than in uncrushed material. Many specimens were collected commercially and lack precise locality data.

media.title: Holotype of Microraptor gui, IVPP V 13352
media.alt: Photograph of the Microraptor gui holotype slab showing the skeleton and surrounding feather impressions
media.caption: The holotype slab of Microraptor gui under normal light, from Hone and colleagues' 2010 study of the extent of the preserved feathers. The white arrow marks feathers; black arrows mark the halo where they appear absent.

materialGroups.label: Skull and jaws
materialGroups.value: Complete but flattened skulls with small serrated teeth, known from many individuals.

materialGroups.label: Vertebral column
materialGroups.value: Complete neck, back, sacrum and long tail with a terminal feather fan; ribs, gastralia and uncinate processes preserved.

materialGroups.label: Girdles and limbs
materialGroups.value: Complete shoulder and pelvic girdles, long arms with three-fingered hands, and hindlimbs bearing the enlarged second-toe claw.

materialGroups.label: Exceptional preservation
materialGroups.value: Pennaceous flight feathers on arms and legs, tail feathers, melanosomes indicating iridescent black plumage, and stomach contents including a bird, a mammal, a lizard and a fish.

specimenCards.title: IVPP V 12330 · holotype of M. zhaoianus
specimenCards.description: A partial articulated skeleton described by Xu, Zhou and Wang in 2000 as the smallest non-avian theropod then known. It anchors the genus name, though its feathering is less completely preserved than in later finds.
specimenCards.meta: Jiufotang Formation, Liaoning · Institute of Vertebrate Paleontology and Paleoanthropology, Beijing

specimenCards.title: IVPP V 13352 · holotype of M. gui
specimenCards.description: The near-complete skeleton described by Xu and colleagues in 2003 that first revealed long flight feathers on the hindlimbs. Its plumage extent was re-examined under ultraviolet light in 2010.
specimenCards.meta: Jiufotang Formation, Liaoning · Institute of Vertebrate Paleontology and Paleoanthropology, Beijing

interpretation.label: Directly observed
interpretation.value: Articulated skeletons, four sets of flight feathers, a feathered tail fan, melanosomes and prey remains within the body cavity.

interpretation.label: Scientific interpretation
interpretation.value: An arboreal or semi-arboreal glider with at least some aerial capacity, black iridescent plumage, and an opportunistic diet of small vertebrates.

interpretation.label: Still unknown
interpretation.value: Whether it flapped in powered flight or launched from the ground, how many species the sample contains, and whether colour varied between individuals.
